title: Designing Agent Systems
subtitle: Build a narrow, measurable workflow before expanding the system
summary: Pip wants a guide that can do everything. The team starts with one ticket cancellation: understand, look up, act, confirm. A narrow useful task makes model trade-offs, context mistakes, and evaluation failures visible before the museum expands the agent’s role.

concepts.title: System components
concepts.body: Pip’s cancellation demo says “done” before anything happens. The model needs instructions, context, tools, memory, orchestration, and evaluation around it. Pip connects ticket lookup, cancellation, and conversation state. The orchestrator waits for the tool’s result before confirming success.

concepts.title: Model selection
concepts.body: Pip tries two models on the same cancellation cases. Capability competes with latency, cost, context length, modality, and deployment constraints. A smaller specialized model may suit this narrow task better than a broad one. Pip compares wrong actions, end-to-end delay, and expense before choosing.

concepts.title: Context engineering
concepts.body: Pip’s guide mixes yesterday’s booking into today’s refund. Context engineering assembles relevant instructions, user input, retrieved facts, and tool results. Pip supplies this ticket and its applicable policy, leaving unrelated purchases out. Conflicting or irrelevant context consumes limits and can redirect the task.

concepts.title: Evaluation loop
concepts.body: Pip fixes cancellations; address changes suddenly break. A successful demo did not cover the whole workflow. Pip observes failures, changes one component, and reruns representative evaluation cases. Both request groups must pass before the next rollout.

misconceptions.claim: System components is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter’s design view combines a foundation model with instructions, context, tools, memory, orchestration, and evaluation. A useful agent is therefore a system assembled around the model, not a prompt alone.

misconceptions.claim: Model selection removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: Choosing a model weighs capability, latency, cost, context length, modality, and deployment constraints. General pretrained models offer breadth; specialized or smaller models may be cheaper and easier to control for a narrow task. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Support architecture under budget
scenario.context: A support agent must answer policy questions and update tickets, but model cost is capped.

options.label: Use a smaller executor with retrieval and evaluation
options.benefit: Controls cost while grounding a narrow workflow.
options.consequence: Evaluation shows the small model handles routine cases and hands edge cases to a reviewer.

options.label: Use one largest model for everything
options.cost: Cost and latency rise and failures remain hard to localize.
options.consequence: A demo succeeds but production volume exceeds the budget.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: A prototype’s largest model is accurate but too slow for the workflow. What should the team compare?
options: Only the highest public benchmark score.
Candidate models on representative tasks, quality, latency, and cost.
quiz.explanation: Model choice is a system decision: the actual task and operating constraints matter.

quiz.question: Which combination describes the core agent system?
options: A model, tools, memory/context, and orchestration.
A prompt and an unlimited output budget.
A chat screen and a database with no action loop.
quiz.explanation: The components together determine what the agent knows, can do, and how it proceeds.

quiz.question: Why define an evaluation loop while designing the prototype?
options: It removes the need to decide what success means.
It exposes whether changes improve the intended behavior.
It guarantees that later production traffic will match the examples.
quiz.explanation: Representative evaluation gives design changes a feedback signal; it is not a guarantee about unseen conditions.
